Parmenides. Around five hundred and fifteen to four hundred and forty-five BCE. He was an Eleatic Greek philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging, eternal, indivisible whole that he called Being. Change, motion, and plurality, he insisted, are illusions. His radical monism challenged every pre-Socratic pluralist and forced all later philosophy to reckon with the problem of permanence versus change.

Parmenides was born in Elea, a Greek colony in southern Italy, and he founded the Eleatic school of philosophy. His only surviving work is a philosophical poem, written in verse. Socrates supposedly met the elderly Parmenides in Athens. Plato dramatized this meeting in his dialogue the Parmenides. Parmenides influenced a line of Eleatic philosophers, most notably his student Zeno of Elea.

His central argument is stark. Reality is One—a single, undifferentiated whole, necessarily eternal and unchanging. "What is, is. What is not, is not." Being cannot come from non-being, nor can it pass into non-being. Being cannot move, change, divide, or perish, because any such event would require non-being, which does not exist. Plurality, motion, and time are illusions generated by the senses. Only reason grasps true reality.

Consider change. Generation and destruction are impossible—what is cannot arise from nothing. Motion requires void, empty space. But void is non-being. Hence motion cannot be. Change requires the thing to be partly what it was and partly what it will be. But this contradicts the unity of Being. Therefore, the phenomenal world of change and flux—what Heraclitus described—is mere appearance.

Parmenides pioneered the method of rational proof. He argued from first principles—Being cannot not-be—to conclusions that overturn experience. This deductive method shaped all subsequent philosophy. Plato and Aristotle grappled with his arguments. Though nearly all later philosophers rejected his monism, they did so by refining his arguments, not ignoring them. Parmenides made the deepest questions Western philosophy must answer: Why is there something rather than nothing? How can change be real? These questions flow from his challenge.
